name: Anomalocaris
fact: Its feeding apparatus was thought to be a jellyfish (Peytoia), its body a sea cucumber (Laggania). Sixteen-thousand-lens compound eyes.
discovery: Recognized as one organism 1985 by Whittington & Briggs. Burgess Shale (British Columbia).
keyResearchers: Whiteaves, J.F. (1892), Walcott, C.D. (1911), Whittington & Briggs (1985)
citation: Whittington, H.B. & Briggs, D.E.G. (1985). The largest Cambrian soft-bodied animal. Philosophical Transactions B 309:569–609.

name: Trilobite
fact: Eyes made of calcite crystal — most sophisticated optical compound eyes in any fossil arthropod. Survived 270 million years.
know: Trilobites moulted as they grew, so most trilobite fossils are cast-off shells, not bodies. Their eye lenses were made of the mineral calcite — the oldest eyes that can still be studied as optics.
discovery: First trilobites at base of Atdabanian, ~521 MYA. Over 22,000 species described.
citation: Whittington, H.B. (1975). The enigmatic animal Opabinia spina. Philosophical Transactions B 271:1–43.

name: Hallucigenia
fact: Scientists drew it completely upside-down for years! The spiky bits are on TOP, not the bottom. And its 'head' end was a mystery for decades. It's one of the weirdest animals that ever lived.
know: Even after it was turned the right way up, nobody knew which end was the head. In 2015 an electron microscope found it: a pair of simple eyes and a ring of teeth — on what had been thought to be the tail.

name: Opabinia
fact: Had FIVE eyes on top of its head and a long bendy trunk with a claw to grab food and pass it back to its mouth. When scientists first showed it at a conference, the whole room burst out laughing — they thought it was a joke!

name: Wiwaxia
fact: Covered in scale-like armor plates and rows of spines — looked like a mobile pincushion! We still don't know exactly what it was related to, but it was definitely one of the Cambrian's weirdest designs.

name: Marrella
fact: One of the most common fossils from the Burgess Shale! It looked like a tiny shrimp wearing fancy feathered armor. Millions of them got buried in mudslides — nature's time capsule.

name: Pikaia
fact: A small eel-like swimmer with a notochord - a stiff rod that is the evolutionary forerunner of the vertebrate spine. Pikaia is one of your oldest known ancestors. Without this humble creature there would be no fish, no amphibians, no dinosaurs, and no humans.

name: Ottoia
fact: A voracious priapulid worm that ambushed prey from its burrow, sometimes consuming animals as large as itself. Burgess Shale fossils sometimes preserve this worm's last meal still inside its gut.

name: Naraoia
fact: A soft-shelled cousin of trilobites that skimmed the seafloor for algae. Unlike its armored relatives Naraoia had no calcified shell, which makes its perfect preservation in the Burgess Shale all the more remarkable.

name: Aysheaia
fact: A soft-bodied many-legged creature that clung to and fed on sponges - the ancient ancestor of today's velvet worms. Aysheaia had stubby claw-tipped legs and moved like a slow caterpillar, linking arthropods to worms in the tree of life.

name: Sanctacaris
fact: Nicknamed Santa Claws by scientists, this was the earliest known chelicerate - the group that would eventually give rise to spiders, scorpions, and horseshoe crabs. Its remarkable frontal appendages ended in five pairs of grasping spines.

name: Haikouichthys
fact: One of the first fishes: a tiny, finned swimmer with a skull of cartilage, gills and a row of muscle blocks — the oldest known animal with a recognisable head and backbone-like rod.

name: Waptia
fact: A shrimp-like swimmer. Some fossils carry clutches of eggs tucked under the shell — the oldest known case of an animal caring for its young.
know: In 2015 researchers counted up to 24 eggs, each about 2 mm, held under the carapace of specimens collected by Charles Walcott a century earlier.

name: Olenoides
fact: Most trilobites survive only as shells. Olenoides from the Burgess Shale keeps its antennae, legs and even tail feelers, showing how trilobites walked and fed.

name: Leanchoilia
fact: Its front limbs ended in long, whip-like feelers. CT scans of Chinese specimens preserved its nervous system — and showed a brain plan like that of spiders and scorpions.

name: Amplectobelua
fact: A cousin of Anomalocaris whose grasping arms worked like pincers, with one long spine opposing the others.

name: Kerygmachela
fact: Half worm, half arthropod: stubby legs, flaps along its sides, and long spiny head appendages. It helps show how the arthropod body was assembled.

name: Archaeocyathids
size: Cups 1–15 cm; reefs many metres wide
fact: Cup-shaped, sponge-like animals that built the first animal reefs — 10 million years before corals did.

name: Nectocaris
fact: A flat, finned swimmer with two big eyes and a funnel like a squid's.
debate: An early relative of squid and octopus — or something unrelated that only looks like one? Each new specimen has swung the argument.

name: Saccorhytus
fact: A tiny bag with a huge mouth, wrinkles, and holes around its body — and no anus. It may have eaten and excreted through the same opening.
debate: Hailed in 2017 as our earliest known relative. Better scans in 2022 showed the “gill holes” were spine bases — it is more likely related to arthropods and worms.

name: Fuxianhuia
fact: An early arthropod famous for its insides: in 2012 its fossilised brain was found, and in 2014 its heart and blood vessels.
know: Some fossils even show a group with an adult and several young — possible parental care half a billion years ago.

name: Vetulicola
fact: An animal in two halves: a stiff, box-like front with gill-like openings and a jointed, swimming tail behind.
debate: Gill slits suggest it is on our side of the animal family tree, near the ancestors of sea squirts and vertebrates. Not everyone agrees.

name: Kylinxia
means: Named after the kylin, a mythical chimera — because it is part one animal, part another
fact: Five eyes like Opabinia, grasping front claws like Anomalocaris, and a segmented arthropod body. Described in 2020, it links the strange early “stem arthropods” to true arthropods.

name: Collinsium
fact: Nicknamed “the hairy Collins monster”: six pairs of hair-fringed front legs for combing food from the water, rear legs with claws, and 72 spines on its back.

name: Tamisiocaris
fact: A relative of Anomalocaris whose front arms were fine combs for sieving plankton — the first known animal of its size to filter-feed.

name: Cambroraster
fact: A radiodont with a huge, flat head shield shaped like the Millennium Falcon, and rake-like claws for sifting mud.
know: Hundreds were found at Marble Canyon, a site discovered in 2012 just 40 km from the Burgess Shale.

name: Hurdia
fact: One of the commonest predators of the Burgess Shale, with a big hood-like shell on its head. Its pieces were first described as several different animals.

name: Odontogriphus
fact: A flat, soft, slug-like animal with a radula — the rasping, tooth-covered tongue of snails. It shows what early molluscs looked like before shells.

name: Canadaspis
fact: A shrimp-like arthropod with a two-part shell, one of the commonest animals in the Burgess Shale.

name: Dinomischus
fact: A cup on a stalk, ringed with petal-like plates, anchored in the mud — like a tiny flower that filtered food from the water.

name: Metaspriggina
fact: One of the earliest fishes, with two big eyes and seven pairs of gill arches.
know: In later fishes, the first pair of gill arches became the jaw. Metaspriggina shows that arrangement already in place — the starting point for your own jaw (2014).

name: Redlichia rex
fact: A large trilobite with spiny legs built for shredding — possibly a cannibal, since bite-damaged trilobites of its own kind are found beside it.

name: Archaeocyaths
size: Cups a few centimetres to 30 cm tall
fact: “Ancient cups”: vase-shaped relatives of sponges that built the first reefs on Earth made by animals. They flourished for about fifteen million years, then vanished.
